title: Split billing window logic and unify export signatures for mid-cycle adjustments
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Several customers are seeing invoice line anomalies (duplicate credit lines, negative adjustments showing as separate lines, and mismatched proration) after late-arriving usage events and rate-limit crediting. Root cause analysis indicates two related problems: (1) export-time windowing logic uses multiple timestamp heuristics (ingest time, event time, and local-day boundaries) which diverge across services and cause the same usage to be bucketed differently for Stripe vs NetSuite exports; (2) export signature/idempotency is not deterministic when mid-cycle proration and reserved-capacity adjustments are applied, so retries and backfills can produce new invoice line items instead of merging with the intended line.

Goal: Reduce invoice noise and ensure idempotent, auditable exports by splitting the export pipeline into a canonical window-normalization step and a deterministic export-signature generation step. This will (a) produce stable bucket assignment for all downstream export consumers, (b) create stable export signatures that survive backfills/retries, and (c) make proration calculations reference a single canonical billing anchor per customer.

Proposed changes:
- Implement a standalone "window-normalizer" service that consumes raw usage events and emits canonical usage buckets with: canonical_bucket_start_utc, canonical_bucket_end_utc, original_event_time, ingest_time, and a normalized_customer_anchor (billing start and timezone). The bucket semantics are per-customer and tied to their billing anchor (not purely UTC day boundaries).
- Move all proration logic to a single export-time proration module that reads canonical buckets and the customer's billing anchor. This module will emit adjustment deltas rather than full line replacements and will attach a deterministic signature hash (sha256 over canonical fields + customer anchor + export-version).
- Update the netSuite/Stripe export workers to prefer signature-based upserts instead of naive insert-on-retry. Add an idempotency index to the export database keyed by signature.
- Create migration/backfill job to rehydrate canonical buckets for the last 3 billing cycles and re-export replacing bad duplicates where safe.
- Add end-to-end harness tests that simulate: DST boundary events, late-arriving rate-limit credits, multi-currency reserved capacity adjustments, and patched backfills.

Constraints and trade-offs:
- Short-term: adding the window-normalizer introduces an extra hop and slight export latency increase for late arrivals. We will mitigate with streaming propagation and a small buffer window.
- Complexity: adding deterministic signatures requires careful backwards compatibility; we'll implement versioned export signatures and a compatibility mode that allows the export worker to accept old (legacy) lines when signature is missing.
- Risk: automated backfills that rewrite invoices must be opt-in per-account in case of customer legal concerns. Backfill will default to a dry-run and manual approval for accounts with enterprise SLAs.

acceptance_criteria: All exported invoice lines for the sampled test accounts (10 diverse customers) are stable across repeated exports and backfills (signature matches on idempotent re-export).
No duplicate credit lines introduced by late-arriving events or retry/backfill flows for the above sample and for a 30-day production shadow run.
Automated end-to-end tests covering DST boundary, late rate-limit credits, and reserved-capacity adjustments are added to the CI suite and pass consistently.
Backfill workflow exists with dry-run mode, manual approval gates for enterprise accounts, and a Console flag showing which invoices were re-exported.
Migration job for 3 billing cycles completes without producing negative net revenue deltas beyond an agreed tolerance (<= 0.1% of monthly bill totals) in dry-run mode.
